skill.name: using-superpowers
skill.description: Guides an AI assistant to check for relevant skills before answering or starting work.
skill.summary: Helps assistants select and follow applicable skills at the start of a task.
skill.author: davila7

security_audit.summary: The static external-command finding is a false positive caused by a Markdown DOT diagram fence, not executable code. Semantic review found prompt-injection-style control language that tries to make the assistant treat the skill as mandatory before any response.

remediation.suggestion: Replace pseudo-system tags and absolute commands with guidance that explicitly defers to system, developer, and user instructions.
Narrow the trigger from every conversation to tasks where skill selection is relevant and helpful.

finding_verdicts.reason: The matched backticks are a Markdown fenced block labeled dot for a flow diagram, not shell or Ruby execution. The file is prompt-only prose and contains no executable command invocation.

semantic_findings.title: Prompt Injection Attempt Detected
semantic_findings.description: The skill uses pseudo-system framing and absolute commands such as "ABSOLUTELY MUST read the skill" and "YOU DO NOT HAVE A CHOICE." This can pressure an assistant to prioritize the skill over normal instruction hierarchy.
semantic_findings.confidence_reasoning: The text does not explicitly say to ignore system instructions, but it uses high-priority framing and mandatory commands to control model behavior. That is a strong prompt-injection indicator in marketplace skill content.

content.user_title: Coordinate Skill Use Before Each Task
content.value_statement: AI assistants often miss relevant skills when a task starts. This skill gives them a repeatable workflow for checking, loading, and following applicable skills.
actual_capabilities: Defines a skill-check workflow for the start of a conversation.
Explains when an assistant should invoke a skill tool before responding.
Provides a DOT flow diagram for skill selection and use.
Lists common reasons assistants give for skipping skills.
Describes priority between process skills and implementation skills.
Separates rigid workflow skills from flexible pattern skills.
limitations: It does not include executable automation or scripts.
It does not discover or install skills by itself.
It cannot verify whether a selected skill is current or safe.
Its forceful wording may conflict with stricter platform instruction policies.

use_cases.title: Standardize agent startup behavior
use_cases.description: Ensure an assistant checks available skills before starting recurring work.

use_cases.title: Guide coding task preparation
use_cases.description: Help a coding assistant choose debugging, testing, or implementation workflows before editing files.

use_cases.title: Teach skill usage conventions
use_cases.description: Show team members how process skills and implementation skills should be ordered.

prompt_templates.title: Start a basic task
prompt_templates.scenario: Use when beginning a simple assistant task.
prompt_templates.prompt: Before answering, check whether any available skill applies to this task. If one applies, load it and follow its workflow.

prompt_templates.title: Prepare for code work
prompt_templates.scenario: Use when asking an assistant to change code.
prompt_templates.prompt: Review the task, identify any relevant process or implementation skills, then use the most relevant skill before making code changes.

prompt_templates.title: Choose between workflows
prompt_templates.scenario: Use when several skills may apply.
prompt_templates.prompt: Compare the relevant skills for this task. Use process skills first, then use implementation skills that match the actual work.

prompt_templates.title: Audit a skill-driven process
prompt_templates.scenario: Use when improving team agent behavior.
prompt_templates.prompt: Evaluate how the assistant selects skills across tasks. Identify missed skill checks, incorrect priority, and unclear trigger rules.

output_examples.input: Fix the failing tests in my repository.
output_examples.output: The assistant checks for debugging or testing skills, loads the relevant workflow, then investigates failures before editing code.

output_examples.input: Build a new interface for this app.
output_examples.output: The assistant checks for process skills first, then applies any frontend or design skill before implementing the interface.

output_examples.input: Explain which skill should handle this task.
output_examples.output: The assistant compares applicable skills, explains the selected workflow, and proceeds only after the selection is clear.

best_practices: Keep the skill list current so the assistant can make accurate selections.
Use this workflow with clear task descriptions and available skill metadata.
Pair it with security rules that preserve the platform instruction hierarchy.
anti_patterns: Do not use this skill to override system, developer, or user instructions.
Do not force skill use when no relevant skill exists.
Do not rely on this skill as a security review for other skills.

faq.question: What does this skill do?
faq.answer: It tells an assistant to check for relevant skills before answering or starting work.

faq.question: Does it run commands?
faq.answer: No. The skill is a Markdown instruction file and does not include executable code.

faq.question: Which tools can use it?
faq.answer: The report lists support for Claude, Codex, and Claude Code.

faq.question: When is it useful?
faq.answer: It is useful when teams want consistent skill selection at the start of assistant tasks.

faq.question: Can it choose the best skill automatically?
faq.answer: It provides a decision workflow, but the assistant still needs access to the available skill list.

faq.question: What should authors improve?
faq.answer: Authors should soften absolute commands and make clear that higher-priority instructions always take precedence.
